cards.headline: Real things, traded on paper.
cards.body: Commodities are physical goods: oil, gold, wheat, copper. Most people never touch the barrel or the bushel — they trade contracts that track its price. The stuff is real; the exposure is a piece of paper that settles in cash.

art.alt: An oil barrel and a gold bar sit on a large crate marked with a date as a figure strains to lift it with a lever — real goods traded in fixed-size, dated contracts.

cards.headline: Two prices: now and later.
cards.body: The **spot** price is what the goods cost for delivery today. A **futures** price is agreed now for delivery on a set future date. Most trading happens in futures, because they let buyers and sellers lock in a price ahead of time.

cards.headline: Contracts come in fixed sizes.
cards.body: A futures contract is a standardised block. One crude oil contract is **1,000 barrels**; one gold contract is **100 ounces**. You do not buy 'some oil' — you buy whole contracts, and the size decides how much each price move is worth.

cards.title: Dollars per one-dollar move
cards.caption: A one-dollar price move is worth **$1,000** on a crude contract and **$100** on a gold one. The contract size, not the headline price, sets your exposure.

cards.prompt: Crude oil rises $2 and you hold one 1,000-barrel contract. What is that move worth?
cards.explanation: Each contract is 1,000 barrels, so a $2 move is 2 times 1,000 — **$2,000**. The dollar figure on the screen is per barrel; your gain or loss is that move times the whole contract size.

cards.headline: The futures curve leans.
cards.body: When futures cost more than spot, the market is in **contango**; when less, **backwardation**. It matters because funds rolling expiring contracts forward keep buying pricier ones in contango — a quiet drag that makes some commodity funds lag the spot price.

cards.headline: Futures are leveraged by design.
cards.body: You do not pay a contract's full value — only a margin deposit, often a single-digit percentage of it. So small price moves swing your account hard, the same magnifying effect as forex leverage. Great when right, ruinous when wrong.
Because a futures contract is a fixed size, a $2 move on a 1,000-barrel oil contract is worth [[1]].
cards.explanation: Multiply the price move by the contract size: $2 times 1,000 barrels is $2,000. The standardised size is what turns a small per-unit move into a large dollar swing.

cards.summary: Commodities trade as fixed-size futures contracts, where standard sizes and margin magnify every price move.
bullets: Spot is the price now; futures is a price for later.
Crude is 1,000 barrels; gold is 100 ounces per contract.
Margin makes futures leveraged, so moves swing hard.

art.alt: An oil barrel and a gold bar sit on a large crate marked with a date as a figure strains to lift it with a lever — real goods traded in fixed-size, dated contracts.

cards.insight: In commodities the headline price is per barrel or ounce. Your real exposure is that price times a contract size you must never forget.
